title: Length Columns
context: Grade 4, and the chapter's first adding and taking away of measures. An adult sees column addition and subtraction, which chapters 2 and 3 taught. What is actually being taught is that the columns now meet at a different number for each pair of units. Beside kilometres the metres take three places, and the page's Example 9 writes seventy-five metres as zero seven five in its table without a word about it. Example 10's Step 3 says the centimetres are regrouped into metres, when its own table breaks one metre into a hundred centimetres. One exercise item borrows ten millimetres for a centimetre, and another carries a metre for a hundred centimetres. Every worked regrouping is at a thousand, except one borrow at a hundred.

writeup.why: Add and take away lengths in two units, writing the smaller unit in its own places and carrying or borrowing by the number that joins the units.
writeup.look: A two-column frame with a unit switch and a joining sign above it, carry chips at its side, and length bars along the bottom.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Length Columns' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the columns worked against the two columns in the frame, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each column's answer lands and the second fixed at two. On the first phase it counts the rows entered against the rows waiting instead. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The unit switch runs across the top of the working area, 520 by 60 at 64,214, with three settings reading km and m, m and cm, and cm and mm, and the joining sign stands beside it, 200 by 60 at 600,214, showing in ink the number that joins the pair set: a thousand, a hundred or ten. The column frame stands under them, 700 by 330 at 64,290: the larger unit's column at the left headed with its unit, the smaller unit's column at the right headed with its unit, a near-black line between them, and the smaller column cut into fixed digit boxes, three for kilometres and metres, two for metres and centimetres, and one for centimetres and millimetres. Up to three rows take lengths, one digit to a box; a rule crosses under the last row and the answer row sits under the rule, with the same boxes. The frame waits until every box of the smaller unit in a row holds a digit, and a zero set in an empty place is grey at full size. Carry chips sit in a row over the larger column, one place each, empty until something is carried. Adding works the smaller column first: its sum is shown in the carry box beside the frame, 250 by 110 at 790,290, as a number of the smaller unit, and each full joining number of it gathers into one amber chip of the larger unit that rises into the chip row, while what is left goes down into the answer boxes. Taking away also starts at the smaller column. When the smaller number on top is less than the one below, that column stays shut and the break control, 250 by 60 at 790,420, lights over the larger number on top. Break strikes that number through, writes the number one less above it in amber, and lays one chip of the larger unit across the line, where it splits into exactly the joining number of pieces: ten slivers for a centimetre, a hundred strips for a metre, and a thousand metres for a kilometre, drawn as ten bars of a hundred. The pieces join the smaller number on top, which is rewritten above it in amber, and only then does the column open. Along the bottom of the working area the length bars run, 1086 by 90 at 64,630, each length drawn to one scale in its colours, laid end to end for a sum and one along the other for a difference, the difference in reddish purple. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across and has no dot key. The answer slot is a two-part measure, the larger unit's number and then the smaller unit's fixed boxes, with the unit names printed beside them, so a smaller part has exactly the places the pair allows, and a smaller column's sum that needs more places has nowhere to go but the chip row. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The larger unit of any pair, kilometres beside metres, metres beside centimetres, centimetres beside millimetres, kilograms and litres, is deep blue wherever it is drawn: its digits in a column, a bar standing for whole units, or a kilogram weight. The smaller unit of the pair, and the part left over after the whole units, is green: metres beside kilometres, centimetres beside metres, millimetres, grams and millilitres. One larger unit carried from the smaller column, or broken into smaller units to borrow, and every digit that move rewrites, is amber. A zero that fills an empty place of the smaller unit is grey. What is left after taking away, and the difference between two measures, is reddish purple. A count of things, handspans, glasses, jars, pourings or bags, is sky blue. The zero mark of a ruler or tape, and the mark where a reading is taken, are vermilion. Water and every other liquid is pale blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every other tick and numeral on a ruler, and every rule, column line, bracket, strike line, table rule and panel edge, is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a unit is told apart by its column heading and its unit name, a padding zero by the box it sits in, a carried or broken unit by the chip it rides on, and a count by the slot that names what is counted, before any of them is told by a colour. Grey never means faint: a zero in the smaller unit's places is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A figure that goes down by one when a unit is broken is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. No measure in two units is written as a decimal anywhere on the stage. The number of boxes and the joining number change together with the switch, three boxes with a thousand, two with a hundred and one with ten, because the largest smaller part the pair can hold, one less than the joining number, has just that many digits. A chip broken on this frame splits into exactly the joining number of its pair, and a chip carried is gathered from exactly that many.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last sum or difference the child worked, with its carry chips or broken unit still drawn and the length bars beneath it.

phases.win: both rows stand with every metres box filled and the zeros at full size
phases.does: types each length into the frame one digit to a box, putting zeros in front of the short metres
phases.goal: each unit has its own column, and beside kilometres the metres take three places
phases.says: The metres column has three boxes. How is a two-digit number of metres written?
phases.check: Away from the screen: write 45 km 7 m and 3 km 260 m in columns. What goes in each metres box?
phases.feels: the metres get three boxes beside kilometres whatever their number, and a short number waits behind zeros
phases.hands: Draw two columns on the board headed km and m, with three boxes under the m. Write 17 km 640 m in the frame, then ask the class to write 6 km 38 m under it. Let anyone who writes 380 under the metres show where the three and the eight went, then fill the hundreds box with a zero. Ask whether six kilometres three hundred and eighty metres is the same length.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many metres boxes are there? Second rung, the phase's: which places does this number of metres fill? Third rung: the row is cut to a number of metres with one digit, and the child fills all three boxes before the longer number comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: digits are written from the left, and the first box is where writing begins.
wrong.move: types the thirty-eight metres of six kilometres thirty-eight metres into the first two metres boxes, so the row reads six kilometres three hundred and eighty metres.
wrong.screen: the row is read back aloud as it stands, three hundred and eighty metres, and its bar beside the card's is drawn three hundred and forty-two metres too long. The three and the eight then slide one box to the right, into the tens and the ones, and a grey zero drops into the hundreds box at full size. The child's row stays drawn above the new one, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the length is said as one run of numbers, and the three boxes take three digits.
wrong.move: types six, three, eight into the three metres boxes and leaves the kilometres column empty, as if the whole length were metres.
wrong.screen: the row is drawn as a bar under the card's bar, six hundred and thirty-eight metres, less than one kilometre beside more than six. The six then moves across into the kilometres column in deep blue, and the thirty-eight go into the metres boxes with a zero in front. The child's row stays drawn beside the new one.

phases.screen: the frame set to kilometres and metres, with two lengths waiting to go in, one with a two-digit number of metres
phases.soWhat: Write each unit in its own column. Beside kilometres the metres take three places, and zeros fill the places in front of a short number.

phases.win: the chip rides over the kilometres column, and the sum stands with fewer than a thousand metres
phases.does: adds the metres, carries a kilometre chip, writes what is left, then adds the kilometres with the chip
phases.goal: when the smaller unit adds up to the joining number or more, one larger unit is carried for each full joining number
phases.says: The metres make more than a thousand. What is written, and what is carried?
phases.check: Add 19 km 480 m and 23 km 755 m. What is written in the metres column, and what is carried?
phases.feels: a thousand metres are too many for three boxes, so they climb over and become a kilometre
phases.hands: Write 1 km 700 m and 2 km 600 m on the board in columns. Add the metres first: one thousand three hundred. Ask how many whole kilometres that is and what is left, then write three hundred under the metres and carry one kilometre. Add the kilometres with the carry and read the sum, four kilometres three hundred metres.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what do the metres add up to? Second rung, the phase's: how many full thousands are in that? Third rung: the frame is cut to two lengths whose metres make just over a thousand, and the child carries before the larger sum comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the metres sum is one number, and splitting a number that has just been made feels wrong.
wrong.move: writes all of one thousand two hundred and twenty-three in the metres column, and gets sixty-five kilometres and a four-digit number of metres.
wrong.screen: the carry box shows one thousand two hundred and twenty-three metres, and a thousand of them gather into one amber kilometre chip that rises into the chip row, leaving two hundred and twenty-three below. The child's four digits are laid over the three metres boxes and the first has no box to stand in. The kilometres are added again with the chip, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: a hundred joins metres and centimetres, and that number is easy to reach for when the joining sign is passed over.
wrong.move: carries twelve kilometres and writes twenty-three metres, splitting the sum at a hundred as for centimetres.
wrong.screen: the joining sign lights, a thousand, and the length bars lay the sum's metres out: one full kilometre and two hundred and twenty-three metres more. Twelve kilometres would need twelve thousand metres, and the bars hold only one kilometre's worth. One chip rises, and the child's seventy-seven kilometres twenty-three metres stays in the slot beside the new sum.

wrong.why: once the metres are written the metres column looks finished, and the small chip over the kilometres is easy to leave behind.
wrong.move: carries the kilometre but forgets to add it, and writes sixty-five kilometres two hundred and twenty-three metres.
wrong.screen: the chip over the kilometres column glows amber, and the kilometres are added again with it travelling down into the sum: thirty-eight and twenty-seven make sixty-five, and one more makes sixty-six. The length bars show the child's answer a whole kilometre short, and it stays in the slot beside the new sum.

phases.screen: two lengths in the frame whose metres add up to more than a thousand
phases.soWhat: Add the smaller unit first. Each full thousand metres is carried as one kilometre, and what is left is written in the metres boxes.

phases.win: one metre splits into a hundred centimetres, the metres go down by one, and the centimetres can be taken away
phases.does: tries the centimetres column, then breaks one metre into a hundred centimetres and takes away
phases.goal: when the smaller unit on top is too small, one larger unit is broken into the smaller units
phases.says: Too few centimetres on top. Break one metre. How many centimetres does it give?
phases.check: Take 9 m 72 cm from 20 m 45 cm. What does the broken metre become, and what is written above the metres?
phases.feels: the metre does not vanish; it moves across the line as a hundred centimetres
phases.hands: Cut a paper strip 2 m 15 cm long, marked in centimetres, and ask a pair to cut 1 m 40 cm from it. Fifteen centimetres are too few to give forty, so they must cut into the whole metre. Write the same take-away in columns: break one metre into a hundred centimetres, so 2 m 15 cm becomes 1 m 115 cm. Take away, and check against the strip that is left, seventy-five centimetres.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: are there enough centimetres on top? Second rung, the phase's: how many centimetres does one metre give? Third rung: the frame is cut to one metre and a few centimetres on top with more centimetres below, and the child breaks the metre before the larger take-away comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: taking the smaller number from the larger is the only take-away that seems to work, whichever line each stands on.
wrong.move: takes the smaller centimetres from the larger, forty less fifteen, and writes thirty-five metres twenty-five centimetres for sixty-three metres fifteen centimetres less twenty-eight metres forty centimetres.
wrong.screen: the centimetres column stays shut on the fifteen on top, and the child's twenty-five is written small beside it. The break control then strikes through sixty-three and writes sixty-two above it in amber, and a metre chip splits into a hundred strips that join the fifteen, one hundred and fifteen. Forty is taken from the hundred and fifteen, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the hundred centimetres are the part that gets written, and the metre they came from is easy to forget to take off.
wrong.move: breaks one metre into a hundred centimetres but leaves the sixty-three metres as they were, and writes thirty-five metres seventy-five centimetres.
wrong.screen: the sixty-three on top is lit with nothing struck through it, beside a hundred centimetres that came from nowhere, and the length bars show the top length grown by a whole metre. The sixty-three is then struck through and sixty-two written above it, the take-away runs again, and the child's answer stays in the slot a metre too long.

wrong.why: six centimetres is one digit, and the first box is where a single digit seems to go.
wrong.move: types seven metres six centimetres with the six in the first centimetres box, as seven metres sixty centimetres, and takes three metres forty-eight centimetres to get four metres twelve centimetres.
wrong.screen: the row is read back, seven metres sixty centimetres, and its bar is drawn fifty-four centimetres longer than the card's. The six slides into the second box and a grey zero fills the first, and the centimetres on top, six, are now fewer than forty-eight, so a metre is broken into a hundred centimetres. The answer comes to three metres fifty-eight centimetres, and the child's row stays drawn above.

phases.screen: the frame set to metres and centimetres, taking a length with more centimetres from one with fewer
phases.soWhat: When the centimetres on top are too few, break one metre into a hundred centimetres. The metres on top go down by one.

phases.win: the centimetre splits into ten millimetres, and the joining sign glows
phases.does: breaks one centimetre, counts the millimetres it gives, and takes away
phases.goal: carry or borrow by the number that joins the two units: ten, a hundred or a thousand
phases.says: One centimetre breaks into how many millimetres? Check the joining sign.
phases.check: Take 4 cm 9 mm from 12 cm 3 mm. How many millimetres does the broken centimetre give?
phases.feels: the same break makes ten here and a hundred one pair up, because the joining sign says so
phases.hands: Count the millimetres in one centimetre on a ruler with the class. Write 62 cm 4 mm less 35 cm 7 mm on the board. Four millimetres are too few, so break one centimetre, and ask how many millimetres it gives. Write fourteen above the four and sixty-one above the sixty-two, and take away. Then ask what a broken metre would have given instead.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which two units are in the frame? Second rung, the phase's: what does the joining sign say? Third rung: a single centimetre is broken on its own and its slivers counted one by one before the take-away comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the only break worked so far in these columns gave a hundred, so a hundred feels like what breaking gives.
wrong.move: breaks the centimetre into a hundred millimetres, as a metre breaks into centimetres, and writes twenty-six centimetres ninety-seven millimetres.
wrong.screen: the joining sign lights, ten, and the chip splits into exactly ten slivers that join the four on top, fourteen millimetres. The child's ninety-seven is laid over the one millimetres box and its second digit has no box to stand in. Seven is taken from fourteen, and the child's answer stays in the slot beside twenty-six centimetres seven millimetres.

wrong.why: the only carry worked so far in these columns was at a thousand, and thirteen is far short of a thousand.
wrong.move: adds twenty-seven centimetres eight millimetres and forty-five centimetres five millimetres, and writes thirteen in the millimetres column for seventy-two centimetres thirteen millimetres.
wrong.screen: the carry box shows thirteen millimetres, and ten of them gather into one amber centimetre chip that rises over the centimetres, leaving three below, while the joining sign glows, ten. The centimetres are added with the chip, seventy-three, and the child's answer stays in the slot beside seventy-three centimetres three millimetres.

phases.screen: the frame switched to centimetres and millimetres, with more millimetres to take away than there are on top
phases.soWhat: Carry or borrow by the number that joins the two units: ten for centimetres and millimetres, a hundred for metres and centimetres, and a thousand for kilometres and metres.
phases.concept: The number depends on the units

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when the unit switch is flipped while a chip waits on the break control. The chip splits in front of the child into exactly the joining number of pieces for the pair now set: ten slivers for a centimetre; flipped to metres and centimetres it gathers and splits again into a hundred strips; flipped to kilometres and metres it falls into a thousand metres, ten bars of a hundred. The joining sign changes with it each time, and the smaller column gains or loses boxes to match. It can be flipped as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the frame is set to kilometres and metres, with two lengths waiting beside it on cards, one of them with a two-digit number of metres. On the second two lengths already stand in the frame whose metres will add up past a thousand, the chip row empty. On the third the frame is set to metres and centimetres, holding a take-away whose centimetres on top are fewer than those below, the centimetres column shut. On the fourth the switch has moved to centimetres and millimetres, with more millimetres to take away than there are on top. The running count at the top left holds the columns worked against the columns in the frame, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the short card, or the metres column, or the break control, or the joining sign, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how many boxes the smaller unit takes. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two or three lengths in any of the three unit pairs, added or taken away, with the carry chips, the break control and the bars open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first: the smaller unit in its places, carrying a whole unit, borrowing a whole unit, and carrying or borrowing by the joining number.

Every smaller unit in its own places, and every carry or break made by the number that joins the pair.

observations.why: Beside kilometres the metres have three places, and thirty-eight fills only the tens and the ones.
observations.soWhat: Write each unit in its own column. Beside kilometres the metres take three places, and a zero fills each place in front of a short number.
observations.observe: Six kilometres thirty-eight metres went in as six and zero three eight, the zero at full size.

observations.why: A thousand metres make a kilometre, so they belong with the kilometres and cannot stay in three boxes.
observations.soWhat: Each full joining number of the smaller unit is carried as one larger unit, and what is left is written.
observations.observe: When the metres passed a thousand, one kilometre chip rose over the kilometres and only what was left went down.

observations.why: The broken metre became a hundred centimetres that joined the centimetres on top, so it left the metres.
observations.soWhat: To borrow, break one metre into a hundred centimetres. The metres on top go down by one.
observations.observe: The centimetres column stayed shut until a metre was broken, and then the metres on top showed one less.

observations.why: Ten millimetres make a centimetre, and a chip on this frame breaks into the number that joins its own pair.
observations.soWhat: Carry or borrow by the number that joins the two units: ten for centimetres and millimetres, a hundred for metres and centimetres, and a thousand for kilometres and metres.
observations.observe: Switched to centimetres and millimetres, the broken chip split into ten pieces, not a hundred.

source_tool.description: A column frame fills the middle of the stage with two headed columns, the larger unit on the left and the smaller on the right. A unit switch above it sets the pair: kilometres and metres, metres and centimetres, or centimetres and millimetres. The smaller column has three boxes beside kilometres, two beside metres and one beside centimetres, and a joining sign over the frame shows the number that joins the pair: a thousand, a hundred or ten. Lengths go into the rows one digit to a box, and a smaller part too short for its boxes goes in with zeros in front, so seventy-five metres goes in as zero seven five. Adding runs the smaller column first. When it reaches the joining number or more, one larger unit is carried as a chip over the larger column for each full joining number, and what is left is written below. Taking away also starts with the smaller column. When the top number there is less than the one below it, the frame will not take them the wrong way round; a break control splits one chip of the larger unit into exactly the joining number of the smaller unit, the larger units on top go down by one, and the smaller number on top grows by the joining number. Along the bottom each length is drawn as a bar, laid end to end for a sum and one along the other for a difference.
source_tool.art_direction: Two headed columns and a joining sign / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a workbench with a tray of everyday things, a fifteen centimetre ruler, a ladder of units, a column frame with a unit switch, a pan balance with iron weights, a tap, jugs, glasses, jars, bottles and a tank.

A ruler is drawn as the page draws it: a long tick at every centimetre and a short one at every half, the numerals one to fifteen, and a first tick carrying the unit name and no numeral. That first tick is the zero mark and lights as one.
Every measure is written with its unit named, the larger unit on the left and the smaller on the right, as in 4 km 66 m. A measure in two units is never written as a decimal on any stage.

The smaller unit's places are fixed boxes: three beside kilometres, kilograms and litres, two beside metres and one beside centimetres. A zero filling one of those boxes is drawn at full size and weight and is never dimmed or dropped.

A number that joins two units is shown beside them wherever the child works with them: ten between millimetres and centimetres, a hundred between centimetres and metres, and a thousand between metres and kilometres, grams and kilograms, and millilitres and litres. Weight and capacity carry one number only, a thousand.
What is left after dividing is drawn in its own slot in the smaller unit, at full strength, and it is never folded into the quotient.

A larger unit broken to borrow is drawn as exactly the joining number of smaller pieces: ten pieces for a centimetre, a hundred for a metre, and a thousand for a kilometre, a kilogram or a litre, the thousand drawn as ten bars of a hundred.
No count, reading or result is shown before the child makes it. A jar count appears only once the pouring is done, and a reading only once the object is laid.
Every word on the stage says weight, the vocabulary box's word, for how heavy a thing is.
A container whose capacity is shown is drawn full to its brim.
Two measures being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a bar, a weight or a liquid the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The larger unit of any pair, kilometres beside metres, metres beside centimetres, centimetres beside millimetres, kilograms and litres, is deep blue wherever it is drawn: its digits in a column, a bar standing for whole units, or a kilogram weight. The smaller unit of the pair, and the part left over after the whole units, is green. One larger unit carried from the smaller column, or broken into smaller units to borrow, and every digit that move rewrites, is amber. A zero that pads the smaller unit's places, as in zero seven five, is grey, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and never faded, because it is holding a place. What is left after taking away, and the difference between two measures, is reddish purple. A count of things, handspans, glasses, jars, pourings or bags, is sky blue. The zero mark of a ruler or tape and the mark where a reading is taken are vermilion. Water and every other liquid is pale blue. Every other tick and numeral on a ruler, and every rule, column line, bracket and table rule, is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because each unit is told apart by its column heading and its unit name, a padding zero by the box it sits in, and a carried or broken unit by the chip it rides on, before any of them is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read the joining sign again, and work the smaller column first.
voice.onNext: A new pair of lengths. Check the unit switch before you type.
voice.opening: Two columns and a joining sign. How many boxes does the smaller unit take?
voice.onFinish: Every smaller unit in its own places, and every carry or break made by the number that joins the pair.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any lengths in any unit pair, with the chips, the break and the bars open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: The number depends on the units

placement.where: After two lengths have been measured with a tape in metres and centimetres, laid end to end on the floor, and the joined length measured again. The tool is what gives the smaller column fixed boxes and breaks a larger unit into exactly the number that joins the pair, which a sum copied onto paper does not check.

answer_key.rule: Write each unit in its own column with the smaller unit on the right. Beside kilometres the metres take three places, beside metres the centimetres take two, and beside centimetres the millimetres take one. A smaller part too short for its places is written with zeros in front, so 75 m beside kilometres is 075. Add or take away the smaller unit first. When the smaller unit adds up to the number that joins the two units or more, carry one larger unit for each full joining number and write what is left. When the smaller unit on top is less than the one below it, break one larger unit into the joining number of smaller units. The larger units on top go down by one, and the smaller unit on top grows by the joining number. The joining number is ten for centimetres and millimetres, a hundred for metres and centimetres, and a thousand for kilometres and metres.
answer_key.wrong: The frame is redrawn a column at a time from the right with the joining sign lit. The carry or the break is made again, one chip of the larger unit laid out as that many of the smaller. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Beside kilometres the metres take three places, so 9 m is written 009.
Add the metres first: 009 and 640 make 649.
Add the kilometres: 52 and 17 make 69. The sum is 69 km 649 m.
items.question: Write 52 km 9 m and 17 km 640 m in columns and add them.
items.checkpoint: Beside kilometres, metres take three places, and zeros fill the places in front of a short number of metres.
items.misconception: Writing the 9 m under the hundreds of 640, which turns 9 m into 900 m.

steps: Add the metres first: 738 and 564 make 1302.
1302 m is 1 km 302 m, so write 302 and carry 1 km.
Add the kilometres with the carry: 45 and 28 and 1 make 74. The sum is 74 km 302 m.
items.question: Add 45 km 738 m and 28 km 564 m.
items.checkpoint: A thousand metres make a kilometre, so each full thousand in the metres column is carried as one kilometre.
items.misconception: Writing 1302 in the metres column, or carrying at a hundred as centimetres would.

steps: 27 cm is less than 64 cm, so break one metre into a hundred centimetres: 52 m 27 cm becomes 51 m 127 cm.
Take away the centimetres: 127 less 64 is 63.
Take away the metres: 51 less 18 is 33. The answer is 33 m 63 cm.
items.question: Take 18 m 64 cm from 52 m 27 cm.
items.checkpoint: Borrowing breaks one larger unit into the smaller units, and the larger units go down by one.
items.misconception: Taking 27 from 64 in the centimetres column because it is easier, which gives 37 cm and a wrong answer.

steps: 3 mm is less than 8 mm, so break one centimetre. Ten millimetres make a centimetre, so it gives 10 mm.
41 cm 3 mm becomes 40 cm 13 mm, and 13 less 8 is 5.
40 less 23 is 17. The answer is 17 cm 5 mm.
items.question: Take 23 cm 8 mm from 41 cm 3 mm.
items.checkpoint: Carry or borrow by the number that joins the units: ten for centimetres and millimetres, a hundred for metres and centimetres, a thousand for kilometres and metres.
items.misconception: Breaking the centimetre into a hundred millimetres, as a metre breaks into centimetres, and writing 17 cm 95 mm.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: 31 km 58 m is written in columns. What goes in the metres column?
items.final_answer: 058, three places, because a thousand metres make a kilometre

items.question: In columns of metres and centimetres, how is 7 cm written?
items.final_answer: 07, two places, because a hundred centimetres make a metre

items.question: Add 64 m 58 cm and 29 m 73 cm.
items.final_answer: 94 m 31 cm. The centimetres make 131, so write 31 and carry 1 m

items.question: Three children ran 3 km 480 m, 2 km 365 m and 4 km 290 m. What distance did they run together?
items.final_answer: 10 km 135 m. The metres make 1135, so write 135 and carry 1 km

items.question: Two long jumps measure 5 m 8 cm and 4 m 76 cm. How much longer is the first jump?
items.final_answer: The first jump is 32 cm longer. 5 m 08 cm becomes 4 m 108 cm, and 108 less 76 is 32, with no metres left

items.question: Take 16 km 875 m from 40 km 230 m.
items.final_answer: 23 km 355 m. Break one kilometre: 39 km 1230 m, and 1230 less 875 is 355

items.question: Add 36 cm 7 mm and 18 cm 6 mm.
items.final_answer: 55 cm 3 mm. The millimetres make 13, so write 3 and carry 1 cm, because ten millimetres make a centimetre

items.question: A child takes 8 cm 9 mm from 15 cm 2 mm by breaking a centimetre into 100 mm. How many millimetres should the centimetre give, and what is the answer?
items.final_answer: 10 mm, because ten millimetres make a centimetre. 15 cm 2 mm becomes 14 cm 12 mm, so the answer is 6 cm 3 mm

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: sets the pair to kilometres and metres, metres and centimetres, or centimetres and millimetres
two headed columns, with fixed boxes for the smaller unit
shows the number that joins the pair: a thousand, a hundred or ten
take one digit each, with zeros in front of a short smaller part
one larger unit carried for each full joining number of the smaller unit
splits one larger unit into the joining number of smaller units
draw each length as a bar, end to end for a sum and one along the other for a difference

teaching_notes: Lay two tapes end to end on the floor before the tool is opened, one measured in metres and centimetres and one in metres, and measure the joined length. Then write the same sum in columns. Example 9 writes seventy-five metres as zero seven five in its table and no step says so; beside kilometres the metres take three places, so say it out loud every time. Example 10's Step 3 says the centimetres are regrouped into metres. Its table does the opposite: it breaks one metre into a hundred centimetres, so eighty-seven metres six centimetres becomes eighty-six metres one hundred and six centimetres. Say what the table does. The summary box names only a thousand metres to a kilometre. Exercise 11.2 then carries a metre for a hundred centimetres in one item and borrows ten millimetres for a centimetre in another, which no example shows. The page's own rule covers both: carry or borrow by the number that joins the two units. The Concept Linking box sends the child back to the opener's throws. Its second question has two differences, one metre eighty-eight centimetres and one metre eighty-seven centimetres, and the second needs a metre broken into a hundred centimetres. Its first question asks for a throw the page never prints, and the honest answer is that the page does not give it.
generation_prompt: Build a column tool for lengths on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A two-column frame fills the middle of the working area, the larger unit's column on the left and the smaller unit's on the right, each headed with its unit. A unit switch above the frame sets the pair to km and m, m and cm, or cm and mm, and a joining sign beside it shows the number that joins the pair, a thousand, a hundred or ten. The smaller column has exactly three digit boxes for km and m, two for m and cm, and one for cm and mm, and a smaller part too short for its boxes is entered with zeros in front, drawn at full size. Up to three lengths go into the rows, one digit to a box. Adding works the smaller column first; when it reaches the joining number or more, one chip of the larger unit is carried over the larger column for each full joining number and the rest is written below. Taking away also starts at the smaller column; when the top number there is less than the one below it, the frame waits, and a break control splits one chip of the larger unit into exactly the joining number of the smaller unit, drawn as that many pieces, the larger top number going down by one and the smaller top number growing by the joining number. Along the bottom of the canvas each length is drawn as a bar, laid end to end for a sum and one along the other for a difference. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put each unit in its own column. Fill every box of the smaller unit. Work the smaller unit first. Check the joining sign. Carry or break one larger unit by that number.
